Where deeds are recorded

The Jefferson County Clerk and Recorder files deeds, deeds of trust and other land documents for the county. Go to the Recording Division in the Administration and Courts building, 100 Jefferson County Parkway, Suite 2560, Golden, CO 80419. The phone is 303-271-8168. Visits can be booked online on the county recording page.

The counter is open Monday to Thursday, 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., and opens at 8 a.m. on the third Thursday of each month. Call before you plan a Friday visit. Otherwise, drop the deed off early in the week, mail it, or send it through an approved e-recording vendor.

Once recorded, a document joins the public record and the county archives. That step is what puts a buyer's name on the title for anyone who searches later. Jefferson County runs from city blocks in Lakewood to canyon lots near Conifer, with Golden as the county seat, but every deed goes through this one office.

Recording fees

Most letter or legal size documents carry a flat $43 recording fee, however many pages they run. A state documentary fee applies on top for transfer deeds with consideration above $500.

Document or serviceFee
Standard document up to 8.5 x 14 inches$43 flat per document
Plats and documents larger than 8.5 x 14 inches$40 per document
Documentary fee on a deed$0.10 per $1,000 of consideration when it exceeds $500
Digital copiesFree
Certification of a copy$1 per document
Documents tied to a death recordFree

State law, C.R.S. 39-13-102, sets the documentary fee at one cent per $100 of consideration. The person who submits the deed pays it, and the clerk collects it with the recording fee. Phone the office for a total before you mail a check.

How to submit a deed

Bring a standard size deed to the counter, mail it, or use an approved e-recording vendor. Large format documents cannot be taken in person and must go through a vendor.

  • In person: standard size documents only, at the Golden office during counter hours.
  • By mail: send the document, the right payment, a return mailing address and a phone number.
  • E-recording: required for large format items. Plats can be recorded electronically only through the county's contracted vendor.

Mail is the slowest route, with returned documents taking 2 to 4 weeks. The county refunds only overpayments of $10 or more, so a short check can hold up the whole filing. Escrow and title companies usually handle this step in a sale. When a deed moves outside a formal closing, the person sending it carries the risk.

What a deed must include

Colorado law requires the grantee's address on the recorded document. Clerks cannot tell you which legal form to use, so have the deed drafted and checked before it reaches the counter.

Consideration matters too. For the documentary fee, property is treated as residential unless the instrument clearly says otherwise. A deed that states no consideration, or $500 or less, can still be measured against the sales price on a related declaration, so understating the price does not make the fee go away.

  • Names of the grantor and grantee as they appear on the prior deed.
  • A legal description, not just a street address.
  • The grantee's mailing address.
  • A statement of consideration, so the fee is figured on the right number.

The Public Trustee and loan payoffs

The Jefferson County Public Trustee handles foreclosures of deeds of trust and releases of deeds of trust recorded through its office. It is at Suite 2510 of the same building, phone 303-271-8580. Public Trustee fees rose under HB 25-1269 on July 1, 2025.

Releases for private trustee mortgage transactions go to the Clerk and Recorder instead, at 303-271-8121. If an old lien was never released, a buyer's lender or title company may refuse to move forward, so check the record early.

Judicial foreclosures belong to the Sheriff, not the Public Trustee. Foreclosure records stay public even after a default is cured or a foreclosure is withdrawn.

Guarding against recording fraud

The county offers a free Recording Notification Service that sends an alert when a document is recorded in your name. Signing up helps you catch a forged deed or a lien you never authorized.

The office will never ask for payment by wire transfer. If an unexpected email or call demands money for a recording, treat it as a scam and phone the office at a number from the county site.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Jefferson County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Wildfire rules in unincorporated areas

Homes in the unincorporated wildland urban interface fall under the Jefferson County Wildfire Resiliency Code, approved March 10, 2026 and effective July 1, 2026. It is not retroactive. It covers new construction and exterior alterations such as additions, deck replacements, re-siding and re-roofing.

A roof replacement covering 25% or more of the roof must be a Class A assembly, and siding replacement of 25% or more must use allowed materials. Smaller repairs, interior work and painting are exempt. The defensible space page describes three zones out to 100 feet from a structure.

A seller in Conifer, Pine or the canyons who starts a roof or deck project before listing can trigger permit steps. Selling as is, without starting that work, avoids them. County staff say no grants are offered, though the SLASH program takes defensible space debris at reduced cost.

A quick pre-recording routine

A rejected or delayed filing costs weeks. Run through this short list before the deed leaves your hands.

  1. Match the grantor's name to the prior deed.
  2. Confirm the legal description and the grantee's mailing address are on the page.
  3. Decide how it will travel: counter, mail or vendor.
  4. Add the recording fee and any documentary fee, then ask the office for the total.
  5. Include a return address and phone number if you mail it.

Other offices a seller deals with

Besides the recorder, most sellers touch three more offices: the Assessor for value, the Treasurer for taxes and the Public Trustee for liens. Each has its own timing.

  • Assessor: real property appeals run May 1 through June 8 each year.
  • Treasurer: taxes are paid in arrears, so 2025 taxes were payable in 2026, and the notice goes out in late January.
  • Public Trustee: any recorded deed of trust needs a release before the title is clean.
  • Recorder: the new deed has to go in with the right fee and a grantee address.

A cash sale to a direct buyer skips showings and lender conditions, which suits a house with deferred repairs, an inherited title or a stack of back taxes. The recording steps above still apply to every sale in the county.

Frequently asked questions

How much does it cost to record a deed in Jefferson County, Colorado?

A flat $43 per standard size document, plus a state documentary fee of $0.10 per $1,000 of consideration on deeds above $500. Large plats and oversize documents are $40 each. Phone the office to confirm the total before you mail payment.

Does Jefferson County, CO charge a transfer tax?

Colorado imposes a documentary fee of one cent per $100 of consideration, paid by whoever submits the deed.

How long does a mailed deed take to come back recorded?

Returned documents take 2 to 4 weeks by mail. Overpayments of $10 or more are refunded, but a payment that is too low can delay the filing.

Can I record a deed in person on a Friday?

Counter hours are Monday to Thursday, 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Call 303-271-8168 before a Friday visit, or use mail or e-recording.

Who releases an old deed of trust in Jefferson County?

Releases handled through the Public Trustee go through that office at 303-271-8580. Releases for private trustee mortgage transactions go to the Clerk and Recorder at 303-271-8121.

The Clerk and Recorder's role in a sale

When a house sells in Arapahoe County, the Clerk and Recorder is the office that takes in the signed deed and any mortgage. Filing the deed puts the new owner's name in the public record. It is also the point where Colorado's documentary fee gets paid. Under C.R.S. 39-13-102, whoever hands over a deed or other title-conveying instrument for recording pays the fee to the county clerk and recorder, on top of the normal recording charges.

This office is separate from the treasurer and the assessor. It neither bills property tax nor sets values. Its job in your sale is narrow: accept the signed deed, confirm it can be recorded, collect the fee and add the document to the public record. Call before you send anything, and ask which forms of payment the office takes.

The documentary fee

The state charges one cent for every $100 of consideration, rounding a major fraction of $100 up to a full unit. If the total consideration is $500 or less, nothing is due. For a typical house sale, think of it as ten cents per $1,000 of price. Your title company calculates the exact figure and prints it on the settlement statement.

Consideration can be larger than the contract price. The statute counts liens and encumbrances and required charges in the base, so ask how your closing agent figured it. If a single deal covers property in more than one county, each county collects only its share, based on the consideration attributable to the land there, and the person recording the instrument divides the total among the counties.

The county sets the per-document recording charge separately, and that amount is not covered here. Ask the Arapahoe County Clerk and Recorder for the current figure.

Residential or not: how Colorado decides

Colorado treats a property as residential unless the deed carries a conspicuous statement that it is not to be regarded as residential. The statement has to be on the instrument when it is signed, and cannot be added afterward.

  • Residential: consideration is the amount shown on the conveyance document. If that amount is missing or $500 or less, and a declaration was filed under section 39-14-102, the total sales price on the declaration is used.
  • Commercial or industrial: the full sales price is treated as paid for the real property, unless separate consideration for personal property appears on the use tax return or declaration.
  • Supporting evidence is neither recorded nor made public. The clerk hands it to the county assessor, who keeps it confidential.

That confidentiality is why a recorded deed can show a fee without laying out every detail of the price. The assessor can still see what the property sold for.

Which recorder handles an Aurora, Glendale or Centennial home

The county where the parcel sits decides the recorder. Aurora spreads across Arapahoe, Adams and Douglas counties. Of its 386,261 residents in 2020, 336,035 lived in Arapahoe, so most Aurora homes are recorded here, but a house in the Adams or Douglas portion is not.

Glendale is an exclave of Arapahoe County surrounded by Denver, and its deeds still go to Arapahoe. Centennial, formed in 2001 out of unincorporated Arapahoe County, is also an Arapahoe city.

CityWhere the deed is recorded
Littleton (county seat)Arapahoe County
CentennialArapahoe County
EnglewoodArapahoe County
Glendale (surrounded by Denver)Arapahoe County
Aurora, Arapahoe portionArapahoe County
Aurora, Adams or Douglas portionAdams or Douglas County

Old deeds and county lines

Arapahoe County was one of Colorado's 17 original counties, organized in 1861, and it once covered a much larger area. Adams County was cut from part of it in 1901, with the formal start delayed until November 15, 1902. A deed for land now in Adams County may therefore carry old Arapahoe County references.

Working from an inherited paper file? Find the parcel's current county instead of trusting the county named in an older document. Cities have shifted too: Centennial did not exist before 2001, and Aurora began as Fletcher in 1891 before taking the Aurora name in 1928. Verify the county from the parcel record, not the city in a mailing address.

Check these before the deed is recorded

Three things change the fee or send a document to the wrong office: the consideration, the classification and the county.

  • The price stated on the deed, and whether liens or required charges are counted in it.
  • Whether the deed says the property is not residential. Silence means residential.
  • Which county holds the parcel, especially for Aurora.
  • Whether more than one county is involved, in which case the person recording splits the consideration.
  • A copy of the recorded deed once it comes back, for your files.

The non-residential statement cannot be added to a signed document later, so raise any classification question before you sign. Your title or escrow company can explain how it handles the fee at closing.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Arapahoe County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Walking through a closing

Here is the usual order of events when a house sells. You and the buyer sign the contract, and the title company opens an order and researches the parcel. Near closing, you sign the deed, and the closing agent works out the documentary fee from the consideration. The agent then delivers the deed to the Clerk and Recorder, which records it. Once the deed is recorded, the sale is public and funds are released.

If you owe back property tax, the title company pays it from your proceeds, so the recording office is not where that gets settled. Taxes go to the treasurer. The recorder only handles the deed itself. Bring a government photo ID to the signing, and keep copies of the contract, the settlement statement and the recorded deed together in one folder. If anything about the price, the lien payoffs or the property classification looks off on the settlement statement, ask the closing agent to explain it before you sign, because changing a deed after it is recorded is far harder than fixing it first.

A cash buyer follows the same recording steps. What changes is the timeline: with no lender, there is no loan underwriting to wait for, so a clean closing date is easier to hold when you are relocating for a job or settling an estate.

Selling in a county that stretches across the metro area

Arapahoe County mixes some of the densest suburbs on the Front Range with open plains, so sellers rarely face the same situation twice. It runs about 72 miles long and only a few miles wide in places. Strasburg, Deer Trail and Byers on the east side have their own school districts, while the west side splits among Littleton, Englewood, Sheridan and Cherry Creek.

  • Confirm the county before you choose a recorder or treasurer.
  • Ask the title company for the recording instructions it will follow.
  • Budget for the documentary fee in addition to recording charges.
  • Keep the closing statement, since the assessor receives sale details from the clerk.

Frequently asked questions

What is the documentary fee in Colorado?

One cent per $100 of consideration, or ten cents per $1,000. Nothing is owed on $500 or less. It is paid when the deed is offered for recording.

Who collects the documentary fee in Arapahoe County?

The Arapahoe County Clerk and Recorder collects it when a deed or other title-conveying instrument is offered for recording.

Is my deed treated as residential or commercial?

Residential by default. It counts as non-residential only if the deed says so conspicuously at signing.

Do Aurora houses always record in Arapahoe County?

No. Aurora lies in Arapahoe, Adams and Douglas counties, and a deed is recorded in the county where the parcel is located.

Where can I get the current per-document recording fee?

Ask the Arapahoe County Clerk and Recorder directly, since the amount can change.

What the Douglas County recording office does

Permanent public documents, mostly real estate records, are recorded, indexed, copied and preserved by the Recording Division. Colorado law puts the deeds and mortgages behind each house sale in the county under that umbrella. The same office also issues marriage and civil union licenses, books first-time passport appointments and posts special district public notices.

When you sell, your closing agent records the deed here. That recorded document joins the public chain of title that the next owner and lender will rely on.

Free alerts against title fraud

A free fraud detection service from the division sends you an alert any time a document is recorded under your name or on your property. It is aimed at title theft, where someone records a false deed. Sign up if you own a vacant house, a rental or an inherited property that nobody visits often, because a bad filing on an empty house can sit unnoticed for months.

Register before you list and leave the alert on while a sale is pending, so you can watch your own deed hit the record. If an alert shows a filing you don't recognize, phone the Clerk and Recorder and your title company right away. A quick call costs far less than untangling a bad deed after a sale falls through.

Office address and hours

The county offices are on Wilcox Street in Castle Rock. For hand delivery and the other basics:

  • Street address: 301 Wilcox Street, Castle Rock, CO 80104.
  • Mailing address: P.O. Box 1360, Castle Rock, CO 80104.
  • Land records hours: Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
  • Checks are payable to Douglas County Clerk & Recorder.

Electronic recording goes through a county-approved vendor and is offered to high-volume businesses, so individuals file on paper. At most closings the title or escrow company sends the deed, which means a seller rarely carries a document to the counter.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Douglas County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Recording fees

Recording a standard document costs $43 per document, and the state documentary fee is added based on the sale price.

Document typeFee
Standard document (8.5 x 14 to 24 x 36)$43 per document
Land survey plat$50
UCC filing, 1 to 2 pages$13
UCC filing, 3 or more pages$18
Death certificates and DD-214Free
State documentary fee$0.01 per $100 if consideration is over $500

Technology surcharges are already built into the county's fees, and the documentary fee is the only charge that tracks the sale price. Amounts can change, so confirm with the office before you send payment.

Getting a deed ready to record

Before anything goes in the mail, read the county's published checklist of recording requirements. In practice, a seller can:

  • Let the closing or title company prepare and submit the deed.
  • Check that the legal description matches your prior deed.
  • Keep the recorded copy and its reception number for your files.
  • Ask the office for a copy if none arrives.

A rejected document can push back a closing date. That is one reason an experienced title company makes a straightforward cash sale move faster.

Recording and the Assessor

A change of ownership is one trigger for a Notice of Value, so a recorded sale can lead the Assessor to send the new owner a notice. Douglas County sends notices only where value, use or ownership changed, which is fewer than 10% of owners. Notices go out May 1 and written objections are due June 8. Business personal property appeals run June 15 through June 30.

  • Assessor's Office: 301 Wilcox Street, Castle Rock, 303-660-7450.
  • County general information: 303-660-7400.

If you sell during appeal season, tell the buyer which valuation notices you received so they know what is pending.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Douglas County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Unpaid taxes and the recorded deed

A lien from unpaid tax doesn't disappear because the deed changes hands. Unpaid taxes can reach the November tax lien sale held by the Treasurer, where the buyer receives a lien, not the property. The interest rate is nine points above the federal discount rate as of September 1, and the current rate is 13%. A deed actually transfers in less than 1 percent of purchases.

Ask your title company to run a tax check before the deed is signed. Any balance gets paid from proceeds, and the recorded deed goes in clean. Property tax is separate from recording, but a sale usually settles both at the same closing.

Following your deed after closing

Here is what usually happens once you sign.

  1. The title or escrow company sends the deed to the Recording Division with the $43 fee and the documentary fee.
  2. The office indexes the document, and it becomes part of the public chain of title.
  3. The Assessor may mail the new owner a Notice of Value because ownership changed.
  4. You keep the recorded copy and its reception number with your closing papers.

If the recorded deed doesn't turn up when you expect it, call the Clerk and Recorder's office and ask for the reception number, then check with your title company. Nothing needs to be re-signed in most cases, since the company holds the original paperwork. Compare the legal description on the new deed with your prior deed before closing day, and ask the title officer to walk you through the other items in the county's checklist so a rejected filing does not delay the sale. Keep copies of everything you sign.

Selling an inherited house

Recording covers the deeds and mortgages for real estate in the county, whatever the type of sale, and an inherited house is no exception. A title company usually prepares and submits the paperwork for you. Heirs should expect the title search to look at every recorded document on the property, so gather any older deeds, loan papers and tax statements you can find before you list.

Vacant inherited houses are the ones the fraud alert helps most. Sign up as soon as you take over, even if you plan to sell in a few weeks.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

State programs that affect a seller's taxes

Colorado lists a property tax rebate, deferral, work-off program, senior exemption and a veteran with a disability exemption. Residential property is taxed at two state-set rates for 2026: 6.8% for local governments and 7.05% for schools. The revenue stays in the county and supports schools, counties, special districts, municipalities and junior colleges. Questions go to the state Division of Property Taxation at (303) 864-7777.

Why recorded records matter near creeks and open space

Highlands Ranch is the largest community in the county, and Castle Rock, Parker, Lone Tree and Castle Pines also generate many recordings. Land near creeks and open space is often described in recorded easements, which is another reason the recorded record matters when you sell. Ask the title company to include any easements in the package you hand the buyer.

Frequently asked questions

Who records deeds in Douglas County, Colorado?

The Douglas County Clerk and Recorder's Recording Division, in Castle Rock.

Is there free fraud protection for Douglas County property?

Yes. The Recording Division offers a free alert service that tells you when a document is recorded in your name or on your property.

What is the recording fee in Douglas County?

$43 per standard document, plus the state documentary fee of $0.01 per $100 of consideration over $500.

Can individuals e-record in Douglas County?

No. Electronic recording is for high-volume businesses through an approved vendor, so individuals use paper or a title company.

What are the land records hours?

Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., at 301 Wilcox Street, Castle Rock. Mail goes to P.O. Box 1360, Castle Rock, CO 80104, with checks payable to Douglas County Clerk & Recorder.

Office location, phone and hours

The Weld County Clerk and Recorder works from 1250 H Street in Greeley. Mail goes to PO Box 459, Greeley, CO 80632. You can reach the office at (970) 304-6530 or crstaff@weld.gov, and it is open Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

One detail matters on closing day. The county's recording FAQ says documents accepted after 4:30 p.m. count as the next day's business, so a deed dropped off late in the afternoon will not be recorded that day.

Recording fees in Weld County

Recording a letter or legal size document costs $43.00 whatever its page count. When a document conveys real property for more than $500, the state's documentary fee is added at $.01 per $100 of the sale price. Weld County adds no transfer tax of its own, so the documentary fee is the only transfer-related charge you will see here.

Document or serviceWeld County fee
Letter or legal size document$43.00 regardless of pages
Maps and plats$43.00 regardless of pages
State documentary fee (C.R.S. 39-13-102)$.01 per $100 if the price is over $500
Real estate UCC, electronic$8.00
Real estate UCC, paper$13.00 for 1-2 pages, $18.00 for 3 or more
Death certificate recordingNo charge
Regular copies, in office or by mail$.25 per page
Certified copy$.25 per page plus $1.00 per document

The fee schedule is set by statute. Documents that arrive with too little money come back unrecorded. Make checks payable to the Weld County Clerk and Recorder or to WCCR, and sign them.

What a deed needs before the clerk will accept it

Rejected documents almost always trace back to the short list below. The county's recording page lays out what to check.

  • Margins: at least one inch at the top and bottom and half an inch on the left and right (C.R.S. 30-10-406(3)(a)).
  • Grantee address: every deed carries the grantee's legal mailing address (C.R.S. 38-35-109(2)), because that address is where future tax statements go.
  • Legibility: a poor original makes a poor public record, and an illegible document is recorded as received with a clerk's note.
  • Return address: mark where the recorded original should be sent.
  • Order: when you submit several documents, stack them in the order you want them recorded.
  • No personal data: recorded documents are public, so keep Social Security numbers and similar details off them.

Clerks do not give legal advice, prepare or notarize documents, or keep blank forms on hand. Recording a document also does not make it legal or authentic, so have the deed drawn up by a title company or attorney.

Which county should record my deed?

The county where the land lies records the deed. Weld's own page cautions that a document sent to the wrong county is not rejected, and the recording fees are not refunded. Check the legal description and the county before anything goes in the mail.

This comes up often in Weld because several towns cross county lines. Windsor, Johnstown, Erie, Berthoud, Lochbuie, Longmont, Brighton, Northglenn and Thornton each have a portion in a neighboring county. A Windsor parcel might be in Weld or in Larimer, and that county's recorder takes the deed.

Finding an owner or a recorded document

Ownership lookups go through the County Assessor, whose website has a Property Information and Mapping section. The Assessor is at 1400 N 17th Avenue in Greeley, phone (970) 353-3845. Recorded documents are searched through the county's self-service website.

The online index search is free. Viewing and printing images costs money, charged either by monthly fee or per document. Online copies are $.50 for the first page and $.25 for each added page, and a certified online copy adds $1.00 per document. Sellers sometimes pull the recorded vesting deed to confirm how title is held, and that search is a good first step when an inherited house has no clear paperwork. Staff can point you to the self-service site if you get stuck.

Releasing a deed of trust and paying the tax bill

Neither of those jobs falls to the recorder. The Weld County Public Trustee releases a deed of trust, and the Weld County Treasurer answers tax questions. Both are in the building at 1400 N. 17th Avenue in Greeley, reachable at (970) 400-3290.

When a loan is paid off at a sale, the lender's release goes through the Public Trustee, and the title company usually tracks it. A change of name on the tax roll follows the deed: the Treasurer says a name change can only be made by deed, and the Assessor updates the name once the deed is recorded with the Clerk and Recorder.

Weld County in brief

Weld County covers 4,017 square miles with Greeley as its seat, third in Colorado by area. The 2020 census counted 328,981 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 378,426. Farms and oil and gas share the county with fast-growing Front Range suburbs, so a seller in a small eastern town and a seller near Interstate 25 face different buyer pools, though both record at the same Greeley office.

A cash sale and the recording steps

A cash sale uses the same recording steps as any other. The seller signs a deed, the title company confirms the legal description and the grantee address, pays the recording and documentary fees, and the clerk records it. With no buyer's lender, there is no underwriting or appraisal to wait for, so a cash closing can be scheduled quickly once title is clear.

If you own a Weld County house and want to sell as is, send us the address and we will reply with a written cash offer. If the house needs work, has tenants or came to you through an estate, mention that in your first message. None of those facts changes where the deed is recorded, but they do change what the title company must collect before it can close.

A checklist for closing week

A few habits keep recording smooth. Ask the title company which county will record the deed. Confirm that the grantee's mailing address appears on it. Verify that fees are paid by a signed check made out to the right payee, and aim to have the deed at the clerk's office well before 4:30 p.m. If you are paying off a loan, ask who is requesting the release from the Public Trustee and when you can expect confirmation. Finally, keep a copy of the recorded deed once it comes back, since it is the record of the transfer.

Frequently asked questions

How much does it cost to record a deed in Weld County, Colorado?

It costs $43.00 for a letter or legal size document regardless of page count. The state documentary fee of $.01 per $100 of sale price is added when the price is over $500.

What is the Weld County Clerk and Recorder's address?

The office is at 1250 H Street in Greeley, with a mailing address of PO Box 459, Greeley, CO 80632. The phone number is (970) 304-6530.

Does Weld County charge a transfer tax?

No county transfer tax applies. The only transfer-related charge is the state documentary fee of $.01 per $100 of price on documents conveying real property for more than $500.

What happens if I record a deed in the wrong county?

Weld County does not reject documents meant for another county and does not refund recording fees, so confirm the county and legal description first.

What does a Colorado deed need to show about the buyer?

It must show the grantee's legal mailing address, as C.R.S. 38-35-109(2) requires, so tax statements can reach the new owner.

Where Boulder County deeds are recorded

The Boulder County Clerk and Recorder takes in deeds, deeds of trust, liens, plats and court documents for every property in the county. The Recording Division is at 1750 33rd St., Suite 201, in Boulder. Reach it at 303-413-7770 or recording@bouldercounty.gov.

A sale becomes part of the public record only once it is recorded. The signed deed comes to this office when a house changes hands, and the buyer's lender files its deed of trust in the same visit. Boulder County is about 740 square miles with Boulder as its seat. Longmont and Erie reach into Weld County, and Superior reaches into Jefferson County, so a deed for a house near those lines still goes to the county where the parcel sits.

Recording fees

Filing one document costs $43, a rate that began July 1, 2025, with the state documentary fee added where it applies. Checks are payable to Boulder County Clerk & Recorder.

ServiceFee
Recording, per document$43
Documentary fee$0.01 per $100 of consideration, on non-exempt deeds over $500
Certifying a copy of a recorded document$1
Non-digital copies$0.25 per page
UCC recording, 1 to 2 pages$13
UCC recording, 3 or more pages$18
E-recorded UCC$8
Recording a death certificateNo charge

For any charge not in the table, call the office at the number above.

How the documentary fee works

Colorado charges one cent per $100 of consideration, starting once the price passes $500. The rule is C.R.S. 39-13-102, and collection is the county clerk and recorder's job. Your closing agent works out the figure and shows it on the settlement statement.

The base is more than the sticker price. The statute counts the price plus any lien or encumbrance and the charges paid to make the transfer. It also treats a property as residential unless the deed carries a conspicuous note that it is not. The documentary fee is the only charge tied to the price of a deed, and Colorado adds no separate transfer tax on top of it.

If a house sits in more than one county, the fee is split between the county recorders in proportion to the value in each, with the person recording the deed making the allocation.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Boulder County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to submit a document

Four routes exist: mail, a 24-hour drop box, the counter, or e-recording by a title company. Each one has limits.

  • Mail: send the Recording Division the document, a check and a return address.
  • Drop boxes: 1750 33rd St. in Boulder, 1755 S. Public Road in Lafayette, and 529 Coffman St. in Longmont. Mark the folder "Recording" and add contact details.
  • In person: the counter is open Monday through Thursday, 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., and closed Fridays.
  • Email: individual owners can send a scanned PDF, with extra fees. Brokerages, title companies, lenders and law firms cannot use this route.
  • E-recording: high-volume filers use Simplifile, eRecording Partners, CSC or Indecomm. This is the only option described as same-day.

Drop-offs in Lafayette or Longmont travel by interoffice mail to Boulder, which can add one to two business days. If your closing date is tight, use the Boulder box or counter.

What a deed needs before filing

A deed needs the correct fee, a return address and no personal identifying information, because recorded documents are public. Remove such details before filing.

The clerk cannot pull back a recorded document, and the staff cannot advise you on which document to file. For a house sale, a title company or attorney drafts the deed and checks the legal description. A cash buyer works the same way, with the closing agent handling the recording step.

Boulder County runs a public search site where you can find recorded documents, download free copies and order certified ones. It is the quickest way to confirm a deed or lien before you list. For land that moved to Broomfield in 2001, older records may sit in Boulder County.

What the office accepts

Besides warranty deeds and quit claim deeds, the recorder accepts plats, military records and court documents such as letters and personal representative deeds. An estate sale can therefore be recorded in the same office as an ordinary sale.

Do not mix up the two counters. The Treasurer takes payments in Longmont on Mondays and in Boulder on weekdays, but the Treasurer is a separate office from the recorder. A tax payoff goes to the Treasurer at 303-441-3520, and a deed goes to the Clerk and Recorder at 303-413-7770.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Boulder County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Recording on closing day, step by step

For most sales, the title company handles recording and you never visit the office. If you are handling it yourself, the sequence is simple. Sign the deed, confirm the legal description with your title or legal help, and strip out personal identifying information. Calculate the fee: $43 for the document, plus the documentary fee if the price is over $500. Write the check to Boulder County Clerk & Recorder, add a return address, and choose a route: counter, drop box, mail or, for individual owners, a scanned PDF by email.

Plan around the office hours. With the counter closed Fridays, a deed signed on a Thursday afternoon has little room to spare, while the drop boxes accept filings around the clock. If you use the Lafayette or Longmont box, add the one to two business days that interoffice mail takes. When the document comes back, file it with your closing papers.

A cash sale follows the same steps. What it skips is the lender's deed of trust, so there is one fewer document to record, and there is no loan funding to wait on once the deed is filed.

Common situations for Boulder County sellers

Sellers here deal with high values, mixed ownership and mountain weather. A few situations come up again and again.

  • Estates and inherited houses, where court documents may need recording.
  • Rentals with tenants, and licensing steps that change when ownership changes.
  • Back property tax, which the title company pays out of proceeds.
  • Houses in areas hit by the 2013 floods or the Marshall Fire of December 30, 2021, where the history is part of the buyer's questions. A deed for a fire-damaged lot is recorded the same way as any other, and the same fees apply.

Before closing, make sure you have a plan for each one. Ask the title company who will record, when, and in which office, and keep the recorded deed when it comes back.

Frequently asked questions

How much does it cost to record a deed in Boulder County?

The recording fee is $43 per document as of July 1, 2025. If the price is over $500, add the state documentary fee of one cent per $100 of consideration.

Is the Boulder County recorder open on Fridays?

No. The office is open Monday through Thursday from 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. and is closed Fridays. The three 24-hour drop boxes stay available.

Does Colorado charge a transfer tax on a house sale?

Colorado charges a documentary fee on deeds, not a separate transfer tax. It is one cent per $100 of consideration over $500, collected when the deed is recorded.

Can I e-record my own deed in Boulder County?

Individual owners can email a scanned PDF for a fee. E-recording through Simplifile, eRecording Partners, CSC or Indecomm is meant for high-volume filers such as title companies.

Where can I find an old Boulder County deed?

Use the county's public search site to find recorded documents, download free copies and order certified copies for $1. Land that moved to Broomfield in 2001 may have older records here.

Where Denver deeds are recorded

If your house is inside Denver, its deed and any deed of trust are filed with the Recording Division of the Denver Clerk and Recorder, 200 W. 14th Ave., Denver, CO 80204. Remote service covers most needs, and walk-ins need an appointment. Arrive over ten minutes late and the staff may ask you to reschedule.

Because Denver is a consolidated city and county, the Public Trustee, who runs foreclosures and handles releases of deeds of trust, works for the same government.

Recording fees

A standard document costs $43. Other common charges:

Document or serviceFee
Standard document$43 per document
Certified copy$1 certification plus $0.25 per page
Release of deed of trust$73 total, including a $30 Public Trustee fee
UCC statement, 1 to 2 pages$13
UCC statement, 3 or more pages$18
UCC statement, e-recorded$8
Federal tax lien$43
DD-214 military dischargeFree
Documentary fee on conveyances$0.10 per $1,000, none under $500

Fees are scheduled to rise on July 1 under a new state law, so confirm the current amount with the office before you mail a check.

Documentary fee on a sale

The only charge that follows the sale price is the documentary fee on real estate grants and conveyances. It is $0.10 per $1,000 of the price, and amounts under $500 owe nothing. Your closing agent calculates it and collects it, so it appears as a line on the settlement statement.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Denver County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to submit a deed

E-recording is the fast route. Denver says mailed documents can take 7 to 10 days, while an e-recorded one goes through in minutes. Your options:

  • E-recording through the approved vendors, EPN and CSC.
  • Mail: the document, a self-addressed envelope and a check or money order payable to Manager of Finance.
  • In person: cash, check, money order or a Mastercard, Visa or Discover card. Temporary checks are not accepted.
  • By phone: the office cannot take card information this way.

Few sellers file anything themselves. The title or escrow company records the deed as part of closing.

Formatting rules

A recordable document needs a one-inch top margin and half-inch side margins under C.R.S. 30-10-406(3)(a), and the largest paper size is 24 by 36 inches. Surveys must be on paper, and a non-paper survey adds a $5 per page paper copy fee. Liens must be notarized before you send them. Staff can't give legal advice or help fill out forms.

One rule catches people out: Denver cannot reject or refund a document recorded in the wrong county, so the person submitting it has to pick the right county.

Releasing a deed of trust

When a loan is paid off or refinanced, the Public Trustee processes the release. The lender or title company files it, and the recorded release then appears in Denver's recorded document search.

You need three items: a signed and notarized Release of Deed of Trust, the deed of trust itself, and the original promissory note marked paid or cancelled. File electronically through Simplifile or Corporation Service Company, or mail by certified mail if you cannot.

An old loan that was paid years ago but never released can slow a closing. Ask the title company to search for unreleased deeds of trust at the start.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Denver County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Satisfaction of a judgment

Clearing a recorded judgment takes steps in two offices:

  1. Mail the Acknowledgment of Satisfaction to the Denver District Court Clerk at 1437 Bannock St., Room 256, with a $20 certificate fee by cashier's check or money order and a stamped return envelope.
  2. Send the certificate to the Clerk and Recorder with the $43 recording fee and a self-addressed envelope.
  3. Send copies of the recorded certificate to the three credit bureaus, because the Recorder does not report to them.

A judgment lien left on record against a house will show up in the title search at closing.

What the recording step looks like at closing

At closing, the title company files the deed, the release of your old deed of trust and the buyer's paperwork, and each then appears in Denver's online recorded document database. Delays usually come from an unreleased deed of trust, a recorded judgment, a tax lien or, on an inherited house, a missing beneficiary deed or proof of death.

Fix these before listing, or before you accept an offer, and the closing date stays put. If you want a written cash offer on a Denver County house with a title problem, an unreleased loan or a tax balance, call us and we will look at it as is.

The Public Trustee's role

When a property secures a loan, the Public Trustee holds title in trust. Its two main jobs are running foreclosures, including auction sales when needed, and executing releases of deeds of trust so that paid-off mortgage liens come off the record. The office has a resource section for homeowners whose house sold at auction.

For a seller, the second job matters most. Your lender's release is what proves the old loan is gone, and the buyer's title insurer will want to see it recorded or in line to be recorded at closing.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Before you list the house

A short checklist saves trouble later:

  1. Ask the title company to run a search on your address in Denver's recorded document database.
  2. Look for an unreleased deed of trust from a loan you paid off, a recorded judgment, a tax lien and, if you inherited the house, a beneficiary deed or proof of death.
  3. Start any release or satisfaction process right away, since the judgment steps involve two offices and mail time.
  4. Confirm the fee amounts if your closing falls near July 1.

Anything you clear before an offer arrives is one less item that can push your closing date.

If a problem does surface mid-sale, don't panic. Title companies deal with unreleased loans and old judgments all the time, and most can be resolved with a phone call to the lender or a filing like the ones described above. Just give the title officer the paperwork as soon as you have it.

Beneficiary deeds

A Colorado beneficiary deed is recorded with the Denver Clerk and Recorder, and it must be recorded before the owner dies. The statute requires recording in the county where the property sits, and the sample form warns in capitals that an unrecorded deed does not work (C.R.S. 15-15-404). The standard $43 recording fee applies. A revocation is also recorded with the clerk and recorder in the property's county under 15-15-405.

When a Denver owner has died and a buyer wants to purchase, the title company searches this same record for a beneficiary deed, a later revocation or any other recorded claim.

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Denver County Clerk and Recorder?

The Recording Division is at 200 W. 14th Ave., Denver, CO 80204. In-person service requires an appointment, and mail and electronic submission are also available.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Denver?

$43 per document, plus the documentary fee of $0.10 per $1,000 on conveyances where it applies. Fees are scheduled to change on July 1, so confirm the current amount.

Can I e-record a deed in Denver?

Yes. The county recommends it and uses EPN and CSC as approved vendors. E-recording takes minutes, against 7 to 10 days for mail.

What is the fee for releasing a deed of trust in Denver?

$73 total, which covers the $43 recording fee and a $30 Public Trustee execution fee.

What happens if I record a deed in the wrong county?

Denver County cannot reject or refund a document recorded in the wrong county, so the person submitting it must pick the correct one.

What the Clerk and Recorder does in a house sale

When a house is sold, the El Paso County Clerk and Recorder files the deed that moves it from seller to buyer, along with the deed of trust and the release that go with a mortgage. The office also collects the state documentary fee at the moment the deed is filed.

Filing is what puts the sale in the public record, and until a deed is recorded the county records still show the old owner. Most sellers never visit, because the title or settlement company handles the filing after closing. Still, it helps to know what the office charges and why a filing can bounce back. Questions go to the recording department at (719) 520-6200 or recweb@elpasoco.com.

Recording fees

Since July 1, 2025, El Paso County charges a flat $43 to record a standard document, whatever the page count. On a deed that transfers title for more than $500, the state documentary fee is added at one cent for every $100 of the price.

The $43 breaks down as a $40 state-set flat fee, a $1 Electronic Recording Technology Board surcharge and a $2 electronic filing surcharge. The change follows House Bill 24-1269.

Document or serviceFee
Standard, oversized, plat or condo document$43 flat, any page count
Documentary fee on a deed (C.R.S. 39-13-102)$0.01 per $100 of consideration, when consideration is above $500
Land survey$43 per document plus a $10 County Surveyor fee
Copies of recorded documents$0.25 per page, certified copy $1 more per document
Plat map copies$3 per page
DD Form 214 and death documents in the real estate recordsNo fee
State unemployment, sales and use tax liens; child support liensNo fee

Copies returned by mail carry a handling fee on top of the per-page charge: $1.25 for 1 to 10 pages, $2.00 for 11 to 20 pages, and $2.50 for 21 to 60 pages.

Getting a deed to the recorder

You can use the drop box, the mail or eRecording. A seller dealing with a cash buyer usually leaves this to the closing company.

  • Drop box: outside the east entrance of the main office at the Citizens Service Center, 1675 W. Garden of the Gods Road. Seal the envelope, enclose payment and add a phone number.
  • Mail: El Paso County Clerk & Recorder, Attn: Recording, P.O. Box 2007, Colorado Springs, CO 80901-2007. Put the return address on the front of the document.
  • eRecording: the county's eRecording software page covers online submission.

To get a copy of a recorded document, email copyrequests@elpasoco.com. Copy requests are answered within 48 hours, and documents recorded before 1996 are held only at the Citizens Service Center.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your El Paso County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Why deeds get rejected

Most rejections come from small errors on the county's recording checklist, and a rejected deed delays the date the buyer appears in the public record.

  • Wrong fee. Recording fees are set by statute, and the county can reject a filing with the wrong amount or page count.
  • Missing documentary fee. Any exemption has to be claimed on the face of the document, or the fee is due. The consideration figure must match on the deed and the transfer declaration.
  • No grantee address. Colorado law (C.R.S. 38-35-109(2)) requires the buyer's mailing address on the deed, because it decides where future tax statements are sent.
  • Margins. C.R.S. 30-10-406(3)(a) calls for a one inch top margin and half inch left, right and bottom margins.
  • Check problems. Checks go to the El Paso County Clerk, must be signed and must not be stale dated. A bad check sends back every document stapled to it.
  • Faint notary seals. An embossed seal that is not inked will not show on the scanned image.

Offices and hours

Recording is handled at the main office on weekdays, and the north branch takes recordings on Saturday mornings. The other branches deal with motor vehicle and driver's license business.

  • Main office, Citizens Service Center, 1675 W. Garden of the Gods Rd.: Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
  • North, Union Town Center branch, 8830 N. Union Blvd.: Saturday, 8:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. for recording.
  • Southeast, Powers branch, 5650 Industrial Place: motor vehicle only.
  • Fort Carson branch, Bldg 1525, 6351 Wetzel Ave.: motor vehicle only.

What the recorder does not do

The recorder doesn't search titles or fix ownership questions. Under C.R.S. 30-10-101(2.5c), the office is not required to search the real estate records to find a document for copying or any other purpose. Other steps belong elsewhere:

  • Releases of deed of trust go through the El Paso County Public Trustee first, at 1675 West Garden of the Gods Road, Suite 2100, before they are recorded.
  • Property tax status certificates come from the County Treasurer. A Certificate of Taxes Due costs $10.
  • If a recorded change of title doesn't show up in the assessment records after several weeks, call the County Assessor at (719) 520-6600.
  • A title company can supply an Ownership and Encumbrances report showing the current owner and any open liens.
  • Wills, probate and small estate forms are handled by the Fourth Judicial District Court at 270 S. Tejon St.

Inherited houses are common here. If a parent's name is still on the deed, updating it is a separate recording, and the clerk advises using a title company or attorney to pick the right instrument.

Protecting yourself from deed fraud

The clerk suggests checking the county records at least once a year for deeds or mortgages you did not sign. That matters most for vacant houses, rentals run from out of town and properties in an estate.

  • Search the recording website, www.epcrecords.com, once a year.
  • Make sure the Assessor has the right mailing address for you.
  • Call the Assessor and Treasurer if tax bills stop arriving.
  • Check a vacant property often, or ask someone you trust to do it.
  • Update the deed when a family member dies and someone else inherits.

El Paso County for a home seller

El Paso County is the most populous county in Colorado, with 730,395 residents at the 2020 census, and Colorado Springs is its seat. It covers 2,130 square miles and was one of the original 17 Colorado counties, created on November 1, 1861.

Incorporated municipalities are Colorado Springs, Fountain, Manitou Springs, Monument, Palmer Lake and Calhan. Falcon, Eastonville, Ramah and Yoder are unincorporated, so a rural or edge-of-county home can sit outside any city. Check which jurisdiction your house is in before you quote a service or fee to a buyer.

Frequently asked questions

How much does El Paso County charge to record a deed?

A flat $43 per document since July 1, 2025, plus a documentary fee of one cent per $100 of price on deeds over $500. Releases of deed of trust go through the Public Trustee first.

Can I e-record a deed in El Paso County as an individual?

The county's recording page links to eRecording software for online filing. For a single deed, the drop box, the mail or your closing company are the simplest routes.

How long does it take to get a copy of a recorded deed?

Emailed copy requests are answered within 48 hours. Copies are $0.25 per page, and a certified copy costs $1 more per document.

Who pays the documentary fee on a house sale?

Colorado law puts the fee on whoever offers the deed for recording. Who covers it in a given sale depends on the purchase contract, so check the contract and ask your closing company.

Where is the El Paso County recording office?

The main office is in the Citizens Service Center at 1675 W. Garden of the Gods Road, open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The Union Town Center branch at 8830 N. Union Blvd. also takes recordings on Saturdays from 8:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m.
